lchf-diet.short: Low-carbohydrate, high-fat diet: most energy comes from fat and little from carbohydrate. Its strictest form is the ketogenic diet.

ketogenic-diet.short: A diet so low in carbohydrate (usually under 50 g a day, with 75–80% of energy from fat) that the liver makes ketone bodies in large amounts.

ketone-bodies.short: Small fuel molecules, such as β-hydroxybutyrate, that the liver makes from fat when carbohydrate is scarce. Heart, brain and muscle can burn them.

fat-adaptation.short: The changes in muscle after days to weeks on a high-fat diet: it burns much more fat, and less carbohydrate, at the same intensity.

pdh.short: The enzyme that commits carbohydrate to being burned: inside the mitochondria it turns pyruvate (from glycolysis) into acetyl-CoA. Its activity sets how fast carbohydrate can be oxidised.

exogenous-ketones.short: Ketone bodies taken as a drink or supplement (ketone esters or ketone salts), rather than made by the body.

carbohydrate-availability.short: Whether the carbohydrate eaten, and when, covers what the muscles and brain need for the training of the day (high) or falls short of it (low).

train-low.short: Doing selected sessions with low carbohydrate availability on purpose, to boost the training signal in muscle. Races are still done fully fuelled ('train low, compete high').

twice-a-day-training.short: Two sessions a few hours apart with no carbohydrate between them, so the second starts with low muscle glycogen.

fasted-training.short: Training in the morning before breakfast. Liver glycogen and blood sugar are lower; muscle glycogen is about the same as after breakfast.

sleep-low.short: A train-low method: a hard evening session, no carbohydrate overnight, then an easy session the next morning before breakfast.

carbohydrate-periodisation.short: Changing carbohydrate intake day by day and meal by meal to fit each session: plenty around hard work, less around easy work. Also called 'fuel for the work required'.

glycogen-threshold.short: A proposed range of muscle glycogen (about 100–300 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry muscle) low enough to boost training signals but high enough to still do the planned session.

bone-turnover-markers.short: Substances in blood that show how fast bone is being built (formation markers) or broken down (resorption markers). They change in days, long before bone density does.
